  • Lost many drawings in a [6] in 1839
  • Was helped in old age by his [7], who was also a talented artist

Questions 37-40

Complete the summary below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
groups.content:
Difficulties and benefits of beehive fences

In dry periods, when there is a shortage of [37], bees may abandon their hives, leaving fields unprotected. Hives can also be invaded by insects such as [38], and some ecologists fear that honeybees may take nectar that would otherwise be used by wild [39]. However, the fences bring advantages as well: the bees can improve crop yields, and farmers can earn money by selling [40].

questions.explanation: Answer: carver Paragraph 2: 'At around fourteen, he was sent to work for a woodblock carver '.
Answer: actors Paragraph 3: 'Most of these early works were portraits of actors from the kabuki theatre'.

Answer: engravings Paragraph 4: he learned about perspective, 'which he discovered in Dutch engravings that had reached Japan through the port of Nagasaki'. Nagasaki is where they arrived, not what he studied.
Answer: sketches Paragraph 6: the Manga series 'contains thousands of sketches of people at work, animals, plants...', forming 'a remarkable record of daily life'.

Answer: pigment Paragraph 7: the prints used 'Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment that had recently started to arrive from Europe'. The note needs a noun after 'imported'; 'Prussian blue' is two words and is the name of the colour.
Answer: fire Paragraph 10: 'In 1839, a fire destroyed his studio, and a large number of his drawings were lost.'
Answer: daughter Paragraph 10: 'his daughter Ōi, herself a gifted painter, lived with him and assisted him in his work'.

Answer: FALSE Paragraph 2: Hokusai wrote that ' from the age of six he had been passionate about copying the shapes of things around him'. He only went to the woodblock workshop at around fourteen, so his interest began much earlier.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 3: 'he published his first prints under the name Shunrō , which his teacher had given him'.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 4: after his teacher's death, 'Hokusai left the Katsukawa studio and set out to learn from as many artistic traditions as he could'.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 7: 'The series proved so popular that the publisher extended it with ten additional prints .'
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 8 says the picture is 'one of the most widely reproduced images in the history of art', but nothing is said about Hokusai's own opinion of it.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 11 says that 'Even in his eighties, Hokusai continued to paint almost every day', but it does not compare the amount he produced then with any other period.

Answer: C Paragraph C explains the fog collectors: ' As the fog blows through, tiny droplets stick to the threads, merge into larger drops and run down into a gutter '. Paragraph B also mentions air, but there water is sprayed into the air to freeze, not collected from it.

Answer: A Paragraph A: a 2023 report warned that ' global demand for fresh water could exceed supply by 40 per cent by the end of this decade'. The 40 per cent in paragraph F refers to how much of Singapore's demand NEWater meets now, not a forecast.
Answer: D Paragraph D: 'a sand dam costs far less to build than a deep borehole and requires very little maintenance'.

Answer: F Paragraph F: ' Persuading the public to accept recycled water was not straightforward , so officials drank it in front of cameras, bottled versions were handed out... and a visitor centre was opened'.
Answer: cones Paragraph B: 'The water freezes layer by layer into giant cones ... Because a cone exposes relatively little of its surface to the sun, the ice melts slowly'.
Answer: mesh Paragraph C: 'Each collector is a large panel of fine plastic mesh stretched between two posts.'
Answer: sand Paragraph D: the river 'carries sand downstream, which settles behind the wall', and 'Up to a third of the volume of this sand can be water, stored between the grains'.
Answer: manure Paragraph E: 'A handful of animal manure is placed in each pit', and 'the manure attracts termites'. Seeds are also put in the pits, but they do not attract termites.
Answer: factories Paragraph F: NEWater is so pure that 'most of it is piped to factories ', while only a small proportion goes into reservoirs for drinking.

Answer: B (Leila Amrani) Paragraph C: equipment ' only keeps working if the people who use it are trained to look after it and have a say in how the water is shared', and projects 'imposed from outside' are likely to fail.
Answer: E (Daniel Lim) Paragraph F: for a small island without large rivers or lakes, ' Managing it well is absolutely a matter of survival for us. '
Answer: A (Karma Angmo) Paragraph B: the stupas 'are not a permanent answer', and ' we will have to keep rethinking the designs for decades to come '.

Answer: C (Joseph Mwangi) Paragraph D: twenty years ago only a handful of districts asked about sand dams, but 'Now, as droughts become longer, we are getting requests from places where the rivers used to run all year '.
Answer: D Paragraph D: ' the fences also have a second purpose: to protect the elephants themselves ', because farmers who lose fewer crops are less likely to harm elephants.
Answer: G Paragraph G ends: if these approaches work more widely, ' beehives may prove to be one of the most promising tools available for helping people and elephants to share the same land'.
Answer: B Paragraph B: ' When an elephant pushes against the wire, the hives swing, and the disturbed bees pour out. ' Stings around the eyes and trunk are painful, so elephants move away.
Answer: C Paragraph C: ' The evidence suggests that beehive fences can be highly effective. ' Njoroge's trial and Varga's study both support this.
Answer: B Paragraph B: ' Once they have been stung, they learn to associate the sound of buzzing with danger '.
Answer: D (Ruth Kamau) Paragraph D: ' The same fence protects both the harvest and the herd. '
Answer: E (Oliver Grant) Paragraph E: ' People may say what they think the researchers want to hear, so reports of changed attitudes should be treated with some caution '.

Answer: B (Amara Njoroge) Paragraph E: ' If only a few farms in a village have fences, the elephants go next door instead ', and the neighbour 'may decide to deal with the elephants himself'. Njoroge also appears in paragraph C, but her comment on this point is in E.
Answer: C (Tomas Varga) Paragraph C: ' Provided the hives are occupied and the fences are properly maintained, this is the most effective deterrent we have for the money '.

Answer: A (Peter Lekishon) Paragraph B: ' Keeping bees for a fence is not the same as keeping them for honey ': for honey you want gentle colonies, for a fence 'lively bees that will defend their hive'.
Answer: flowers Paragraph F: 'when flowers are scarce, entire colonies may abandon their hives'.
Answer: ants Paragraph F: 'Hives can also be invaded by insects such as ants '. Honey badgers also damage hives, but they are not insects (and the name is two words).
Answer: pollinators Paragraph F: large numbers of honeybee colonies 'may increase competition for nectar with wild pollinators '.
Answer: honey Paragraph G: 'Families can also earn extra income by selling honey '.
